raw_case_text: A 26-year-old man with no medical history presented to the emergency department of a local hospital with swelling in the right forearm. The patient had no history of smoking, alcohol consumption, or drug use. He worked as a feeder at a local chicken farm. He reported superficial abrasion on the back of the right elbow 10 days prior to when work. The wound was scarbed after self-disinfection with iodophor. He had manually removed part of the scab 3 days prior (Figure 1A) and subsequently noticed slight swelling around the wound, accompanied by oozing from the wound surface the next day (Figure 1B). On arrival, he complained of progressive swelling and numbness in the right forearm with no fever or chills. Physical examinations revealed oozing of the wound and erythema around the skin of the elbow, with increased skin tension and multiple tense bullae. Movement of the elbow joint was restricted. Vital signs were as follows: blood pressure, 113/62 mmHg; pulse rate, 72 beats/min; respiratory rate, 15 breaths/min; temperature, 36.7  C. Routine blood tests revealed a normal white blood cell (WBC) of 6.02 x 109/L with 63% neutrophils and a normal lymphocyte count of 1.57 x 109/L. Inflammatory biomarkers showed that the C-reactive protein (CRP) level was slightly increased (9.43 mg/L, normal range <8.200 mg/L). All other laboratory values were within the reference ranges. Empirical cephalosporin antibiotics were administered intravenously and the patient underwent emergent fasciotomy. The initial treatment was left open with a sterile dressing (Figure 2A). The tense bullae subsided after fasciotomy (Figure 2B). Wound samples and multiple secretion cultures were negative for bacteria. Six days later, the patient underwent a second debridement and negative-pressure wound therapy was applied to promote healing (Figure 2C). The wound samples were sent for bacterial and fungal detection. Fungal cultures and tissue specimen smear examinations were positive for Aspergillus flavus but negative for bacteria (Figure 3). This result was confirmed in subsequent cultures. Oral voriconazole (200 mg twice daily) and intravenous cephalosporin were administered. Finally, the wound was closed on the 11th day (Figure 2D), and he was discharged with oral voriconazole on the 14th day after admission. The patient had no fever or other vital signs that fluctuated throughout the disease course. During hospitalization, infection and inflammation indicators such as WBC, CRP, interleukin-6 (IL-6), and procalcitonin (PCT) levels were normal or showed only mild abnormalities (Table 1). Serum (1-3)-beta-D-glucan (G) and galactomannan (GM) assays were negative.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 26-year-old male chicken-farm worker presented with progressive swelling and numbness of the right forearm 10 days after a superficial right elbow abrasion.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Ten days prior to presentation, the patient sustained a superficial abrasion on the posterior right elbow while working at a chicken farm and disinfected it himself with iodophor. Three days prior to admission, he manually picked off part of the scab, noticing mild perilesional swelling and wound oozing the next day, which rapidly progressed to severe right forearm swelling, tense blisters, restricted elbow motion, and forearm numbness without fever or chills.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior medical conditions; non-smoker, non-drinker, no illicit drug use; employed as a feeder at a local chicken farm.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right elbow wound oozing, progressive right forearm swelling, tense bullae, restricted elbow mobility, and forearm numbness; negative for fever or chills.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vitals: blood pressure 113/62 mmHg, pulse 72 bpm, respiratory rate 15 breaths/min, and temperature 36.7 C (remained afebrile throughout hospitalization). Right upper extremity exam showed wound oozing and erythema around the posterior elbow, markedly increased forearm skin tension, multiple tense bullae, and restricted elbow joint range of motion.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission CBC was normal: WBC 6.02 x 10^9/L (63% neutrophils) and lymphocytes 1.57 x 10^9/L. CRP was mildly elevated at 9.43 mg/L (normal <8.200 mg/L), while procalcitonin, IL-6, and other routine labs were normal or near-normal. Multiple wound and secretion bacterial cultures were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan (G) and galactomannan (GM) assays were negative. Following emergent forearm fasciotomy on day 1 and repeat surgical debridement with negative-pressure wound therapy (NPWT) on day 6, direct tissue smear microscopy and repeated fungal cultures of the deep wound specimens were positive for Aspergillus flavus and negative for bacteria.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary cutaneous and deep soft-tissue Aspergillus flavus infection of the right forearm mimicking acute bacterial compartment syndrome after traumatic inoculation at a poultry farm, confirmed by direct tissue microscopy and repeated wound fungal cultures growing A. flavus (with negative bacterial cultures and negative serum G/GM). Treated with emergent decompressive forearm fasciotomy on day 1, second surgical debridement and negative-pressure wound therapy on day 6, intravenous cephalosporin, and oral voriconazole (200 mg twice daily), achieving primary wound closure on day 11 and discharge on oral voriconazole on hospital day 14.
